column2: The great army of Brahmanas and kshatriyas that rose up, O Bharata, went to death on reaching you, with horses, chariots and elephants.
The fierce, cruel-deeded Tukharas, Yavanas, Khashas, Darvabhisaras, Daradas, Shakas, Ramathas, Tanganas,
Andhrakas, Pulindas and Kiratas of fierce valour, Mlecchas and mountaineers, dwellers by the sea and in watery regions, eager, keen for battle, strong, firm-handed—
these, in great fury, for Suyodhana's sake with the Kurus, could not be conquered in battle by anyone other than you, scorcher of foes.
Seeing the mighty, strong array of Dhritarashtra's son, what man would advance against it if you were not his protector?
That force, risen like the sea and covered with dust, was split and slain, lord, by the enraged Pandavas guarded by you.
Jayatsena, the mighty lord of the Magadhas, was slain in battle by Abhimanyu only seven days ago.
Then Bhima with his mace slew ten thousand elephants of terrible action and that king's equipment; then other elephants and hundreds of chariots were slain by force.
So, dear one, in that great-fear battle going on, the Kauravas, meeting Bhimasena and you, Pandava, with their horses, chariots and elephants went from here to the world of death.
Likewise when the van of the army was slain there by the Pandavas, Partha, Bhishma loosed fearful showers of arrows, O revered one.
Covering the Chedis, Kashis, Panchalas, Karushas, Matsyas and Kekayas with arrows, he, skilled in harsh weapons, brought them to destruction.
With arrows loosed from his bow, tearing others' bodies, the sky became full of golden-feathered, straight-flying arrows.
At the tenth speed they went and slew horses, chariots and elephants; the wicked, avoiding nine paths, he shot arrows at length.
For ten days Bhishma, slaying your army, emptied chariot-seats and killed elephants and horses.
Showing his own form in battle like Rudra and Upendra, he plunged into the Pandava divisions and scattered them.
Slaying kings, the Chedis, Panchalas and Kekayas, he gradually burned the Pandava army, wishing to raise up Suyodhana.
As he ranged in battle like the burning sun, the Srinjayas could not look at him, nor other kings.
As he ranged victorious in the war, the Pandavas suddenly rushed at him by their own way.
Having routed the Pandavas and Srinjayas in battle, Bhishma alone attained the status of a lone hero.
Shikhandin, guarded by you, meeting that great chariot-warrior, felled the tiger among men with straight-jointed arrows.
There lies the Grandsire fallen on his bed of arrows, having met you, tiger among men, as a vulture meets a crow.
Drona, fierce, for five days destroyed the enemy armies, made an array in the great battle and felled great chariot-warriors.
The great chariot-warrior, like Death, having guarded Jayadratha in battle, fought and burned creatures in the fierce night.
For two days, Bharadvaja's son of great valour, having met Dhrishtadyumna, went to the highest goal.
If you, in the battle, had not held back the chariot-warriors led by the charioteer's son, Drona would not have perished.
By you the entire force of Dhritarashtra's son was held back; thereby Drona was slain in battle by the Parshata, Dhananjaya.
What other kshatriya in battle besides you could do what you did, Partha, in the slaying of Jayadratha?
Having held back the great army and slain brave kings, the Sindhu king was slain by you with the strength and splendour of your weapons.
Kings regard the slaying of the Sindhu king as marvellous; it is not marvellous coming from you, for you, Partha, are a great chariot-warrior.
When kshatra met you in battle, it was tormented in a single day, O Bharata, I think, and not restored.
This dreadful army of Dhritarashtra's son in the battle was destroyed with all its heroes when Bhishma and Drona were slain.
With its best warriors shattered, horses, men and elephants slain, the Bharata host shines today like the sky bereft of sun, moon and stars.
This army has been shattered in battle by the terrible valour of Bhima, Partha, like the asura host of old by Shakra's prowess.
Of them, five great chariot-warriors remain unslain: Ashvatthaman, Kritavarman, Karna, the lord of the Madras and Kripa.
Having slain those five great chariot-warriors today, tiger among men, your enemies slain, give the earth to the king with its islands and cities,
with its sky, waters and netherworld, mountains and great forests; today let Partha of immeasurable valour and fortune gain the earth.
Having slain this earth's daityas and danavas as Vishnu of old, give the earth to the king as Hari to Shakra.
Today let the Panchalas rejoice, their foes slain by you, as the gods when the danavas were slain by Vishnu.
Or if, best of men, honouring your teacher Drona, you have compassion for Ashvatthaman and, from reverence for the preceptor, for Kripa,
or if honouring your very closely related brothers and kinsmen, I shall not send Kritavarman to Yama's abode,
nor Shalya, king of the Madras, mother's brother—if you, lotus-eyed, being compassionate, do not wish to kill them,
then today, best of men, slay quickly with sharp arrows this sinful-minded, mean Karna, ever hostile to the Pandavas.
This is a good deed of yours; there is nothing unfitting here; we too know it and there is no fault in it.
In the burning at night of your mother with her sons, and in all that Suyodhana set going against you at the dice, in all that the evil-souled Karna is the root here, Arjuna.
Suyodhana always thinks his protection is in Karna; therefore, enraged, he even set about seizing me.
The mind of Dhritarashtra's son, giver of honour, is firm that Karna will conquer all the Parthas in battle, no doubt.
Relying on Karna, Kaunteya, the hostility of Dhritarashtra's son with you was chosen, though knowing your strength.
Karna always says, 'I shall conquer the assembled Parthas and Vasudeva with the king in the great battle.'
Encouraging the evil-souled, ill-minded Dhritarashtra's son, Karna roars in the assembly; slay him today, O Bharata.
And whatever sin Dhritarashtra's son perpetrated against you, in all of it the evil-souled, sinful Karna is foremost.
And that of Dhritarashtra's sons, whom six cruel great chariot-warriors—I saw slain the hero Saubhadra of bull-like eyes,
shaking the heroes Drona, Drona's son and Kripa, making elephants manless and great chariot-warriors chariotless,
making horses riderless and foot-soldiers weaponless and lifeless, the bull-shouldered increaser of the fame of the Kurus and Vrishnis,
crushing divisions, afflicting great chariot-warriors, sending men, horses and elephants to Yama's abode,
Saubhadra, striving with arrows, as if burning the army—that burns my limbs, friend; I swear to you by truth.
And even there the evil-souled Karna, lord, plotted against him, Karna being unable to stand before Abhimanyu in the battle.
Pierced by arrows, senseless, drenched in blood, sighing, blazing with anger, turned away, tormented by arrows,
having made up his mind to withdraw, despairing of life, he stood greatly bewildered, wearied by the blows in battle.
Then, hearing Drona's cruel word in the battle, resembling Death, Karna then cut his bow.
Then, with his weapon cut by him in the battle, the five great chariot-warriors and that one of deceitful mind killed him with showers of arrows.
And what Karna said to Krishna in the assembly, harsh words, cruelly, in the presence of the Pandavas and Kurus:
'The Pandavas are destroyed, Krishna, gone to eternal hell; choose another husband, broad-hipped, measured in speech.
With fine eyebrows, become a slave of Dhritarashtra and enter his house; you with curved lashes have no husbands.'
The ignorant of dharma, utterly ill-minded, sinful Karna spoke those sinful words, O Bharata, as you listened.
Let your gold-adorned, stone-whetted arrows, loosed by you, that cut off life, quench that sinner's word.
And whatever other sins the evil-souled one committed against you, let your arrows today quench them and his life.
Let Karna, the evil-souled one, touching with his limbs today the dreadful arrows sent by Gandiva, remember the words of Drona and Bhishma.
Let your gold-feathered, lightning-bright iron arrows, slayers of foes, after piercing his vitals drink his blood.
Let the fierce keen arrows loosed from your arms, piercing his vitals, send Karna of great speed to Yama's abode.
Today let the kings of the earth, crying "Alas," dejected, tormented by your arrows, see Karna falling from his chariot.
Today let his own friends see Karna sunk in his own blood, lying fallen on the ground, his weapons cast away.
Let the great elephant-rope banner of Adhiratha's son, torn down by your broad-headed arrow, fall trembling to the ground.
Seeing his chariot adorned with gold cut by your hundreds of arrows, its warriors slain, let Shalya flee in fear.
Then Suyodhana, seeing Adhiratha's son slain by you, will despair of life and of kingdom, Dhananjaya.
These Panchalas flee, slain by sharp arrows from Karna, who wishes to lift up the Pandavas, O best of the Bharatas.
Know the Panchalas, the sons of Draupadi, Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandin, Dhrishtadyumna's sons, Shatanika, Nakula's son,
Nakula, Sahadeva, Durmukha, Janamejaya, Suvarma and Satyaki to be under Karna's power.
The dreadful roar is heard, scorcher of foes, of the kinsmen of the Panchalas struck by Karna in the great battle.
The Panchalas would never turn away in fear in any way, for the great chariot-warriors, mighty archers, do not count death.
The Panchalas did not turn away from Bhishma, who alone surrounded the Pandava army with masses of arrows.
So too they rushed at Drona, the blazing fire of weapons, teacher of all bowmen, burning, unassailable, with force.
Those tamers of foes, always ready to conquer foes in battle, would never turn away in fear of Adhiratha's son.
As those mighty Panchalas rush on him, the hero Karna takes their lives with arrows as fire takes moths.
Facing him, those heroes who have given up life for their friends' sake, Radheya brings to destruction by hundreds in the battle.
The terrible weapon that Karna obtained long ago from Rama, from Bhargava, best of sages—its form is being displayed.
It scorches all armies, of terrible, dreadful form, and enveloping the great army it blazes with its own splendour.
These arrows loosed from Karna's bow range in the battle like swarms of bees, scorching your men.
These Panchalas range in all quarters, O Bharata, having met Karna's weapon in battle, hard for the unrestrained to repel.
This Bhima of firm wrath, surrounded by Srinjayas on every side, fighting Karna, is being tormented with sharp arrows.
If neglected, Karna would slay the Pandavas, Srinjayas and Panchalas, O Bharata, like a disease spread through the body.
I see no other warrior than you in Yudhishthira's army who could meet Radheya and return home safe.
Having slain him today with sharp arrows, best of the Bharatas, fulfil your vow, Partha, and gain fame.
You alone are able to conquer in battle the Kauravas with Karna, no other in battle, best of warriors; this I tell you truly.
Having done this great deed and slain the great chariot-warrior Karna, be fulfilled and successful, Partha, and be happy, best of men."
Then, quickly wiping the bowstring, he drew Gandiva for Karna's destruction and said to Keshava:

With you as protector, Govinda, victory is surely mine, since you, lord of the past and future, are pleased with me today.
mahabharata:8:52.4	With you as my aid, Krishna, I could win the supreme world for the three assembled worlds; what then of Karna in the great battle?
mahabharata:8:52.5	I see the Panchala army fleeing, Janardana; I see Karna ranging fearless in battle.
mahabharata:8:52.6	I see the Bhargava weapon ranging on every side, loosed by Karna, Varshneya, like Shakra's great thunderbolt.
mahabharata:8:52.7	This is that battle in which what I do, Krishna, will be told by beings as long as the earth lasts.
mahabharata:8:52.8	Today, Krishna, my arrows loosed from Gandiva, driven by my hand, striking, will send Karna to death.
mahabharata:8:52.9	Today King Dhritarashtra will despise his own judgment, by which he consecrated Duryodhana, unfit for kingship, to the kingdom.
mahabharata:8:52.10	Today, mighty-armed one, Dhritarashtra will be parted from kingdom, happiness, fortune, realm, city and sons.
mahabharata:8:52.11	Today King Duryodhana will despair of life when Karna is slain, Krishna; I tell you the truth.
mahabharata:8:52.12	Today, seeing Karna shattered by my arrows, let the lord of men recall your words about peace.
mahabharata:8:52.13	Today let Subala's son know, Krishna, the stake, the arrows, the gambling-hall, Gandiva, the circle and my chariot.
mahabharata:8:52.14	The earth will drink today the blood of the charioteer's son who in battle regards no other man on earth as his match; the arrows loosed by Gandiva will give Karna the highest goal.
mahabharata:8:52.15	Today Radheya will suffer for what he said to Panchali in the midst of the assembly, harsh words, reviling the Pandavas.
mahabharata:8:52.16	Those sesame seeds of eunuchs there, those seeds, will be today, when Vaikartana Karna, the charioteer's son, the evil-souled, is slain.
mahabharata:8:52.17	What he said, 'I shall protect you from the sons of Pandu', my keen arrows will make untrue.
mahabharata:8:52.18	He who said, 'I shall slay all the Pandavas with their sons', I shall slay that Karna today in the sight of all bowmen.
mahabharata:8:52.19	Relying on whose valour Dhritarashtra's son, of arrogant mind, ill-minded and wicked, always scorned us, that Karna Radheya I shall slay today, Madhusudana.
mahabharata:8:52.20	Today, when Karna is slain, Krishna, let Dhritarashtra's sons with their kings flee in all directions, terrified, like deer terrified by a lion.
mahabharata:8:52.21	Today, with Karna slain by me in battle with his sons and friends, let King Duryodhana look to the earth.
mahabharata:8:52.22	Today, seeing Karna slain, let the very impatient son of Dhritarashtra know me, Krishna, as the foremost of all bowmen in battle.
mahabharata:8:52.23	Today I shall be free of debt, Krishna, to bowmen, to anger, to the Kurus, to arrows and to Gandiva.
mahabharata:8:52.24	Today I shall discharge the sorrow stored for thirteen years, having slain Karna in battle, Krishna, as Maghavan slew Shambara.
mahabharata:8:52.25	Today, when Karna is slain in the fight, let the great chariot-warriors of the Somakas, wishing to accomplish their friends' task, think their work done.
mahabharata:8:52.26	I do not know how much affection Shaineya (Satyaki) will have today, Madhava, when Karna is slain and I, superior in the bowstring, too.
mahabharata:8:52.27	Having slain Karna in battle and his great chariot-warrior son, I shall give joy to Bhima, the twins and Satyaki.
mahabharata:8:52.28	I shall be free of debt to Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin and the Panchalas, Madhava, having slain Karna in the great battle.
mahabharata:8:52.29	Today let them see Dhananjaya, impatient, fighting the Kauravas in battle and felling the charioteer's son; and I shall say further in your presence my own praise.
mahabharata:8:52.30	In the science of the bow there is no one equal to me in the world; in valour who is my equal; who else is my equal in forbearance; likewise in anger there is no match for me.
mahabharata:8:52.31	I, the bowman, by the might of my arms bring defeat on asuras and gods and all assembled beings; know my manliness is higher than the highest.
mahabharata:8:52.32	With the flame of arrows and Gandiva, I alone, attacking all the Kurus and Bahlikas, would burn them with their followers by force, as fire burns dry grass at the end of winter.
mahabharata:8:52.33	These arrows are written on my hand, the bow with arrow is set in my left; my feet are with chariot and banner; none conquer one like me in the fight.
The sky with great elephants as clouds, weapon-water, with the sounds of instruments and wheel-rims and palms, gold-painted weapons as lightning, and the noise surrounded by great chariot-warriors,
dreadful in speed, bearing floods of blood, thronged with swords, bearing the lives of kshatriyas, an unseasonal cruel rain of misfortune—that became the destruction of creatures.
Partha brought chariots with charioteers and horses, and elephants, all foes, under the sway of death with masses of arrows, and horses with riders and bands of foot-soldiers likewise.
Kripa and Shikhandin met in battle; Satyaki went against Duryodhana; Shrutashrava against Drona's son; Yudhamanyu against Chitrasena.
Karna's chariot-warrior son met Sushena, Uttamaujas the Srinjayas; Sahadeva, hungry, ran at the king of Gandhara like a lion at a great bull.
Shatanika, Nakula's son, afflicted the youthful Vrishasena, Karna's son, with masses of arrows; and Karna's heroic son the Panchala's son with many showers of arrows.
Nakula, son of Madri, the bull among chariot-warriors, a varied fighter, attacked Kritavarman; the lord of the Panchalas, Yajnaseni's son, attacked the commander Karna with his army.
Duhshasana, O Bharata, and the Bharata force and the Samshaptaka host, prosperous, then met Bhima in battle, best of weapon-bearers, of irresistible speed.
The hero slew Karna's son there, and Uttamaujas cut off his head by force; it fell to the earth, and made the earth and sky resound with its roar.
Seeing Sushena's head fallen on the earth, Karna, in distress, in rage cut his horses, chariot and banner with sharp, well-edged arrows.
Uttamaujas pierced with sharp arrows and a shining sword; having slain Kripa's horses, he then mounted Shikhandin's chariot.
Seeing Kripa chariotless, Shikhandin on his chariot did not wish to strike him with arrows; Drona's son, holding off, lifted Kripa on his chariot like a cow out of mud.
The wind's son (Bhima), with sharp golden arrows, scorched the army of your sons, very terrible, like the sun at midsummer at noon.
Thus urged by Bhimasena, that charioteer went towards your sons' force, the fierce-speeding charioteer going where Bhima wished to go to that force.
Then other Kauravas, with elephants, chariots, horses and foot-soldiers, advanced on every side against Bhima's excellent, very swift horses and struck them with masses of arrows.
Then the great soul cut the coming arrows with golden-feathered arrows; those golden-feathered arrows fell cut in two and three by Bhima's arrows.
Then, O king, in the midst of your force a dreadful roar of chariot-men, horse-men and men struck by Bhima appeared, O lord of men, like that of mountains struck by thunderbolts.
Being slain, those chief kings, pierced by the foremost of Bhimasena's arrows, attacked Bhima on every side in battle, as birds a tree for flowers.
Then he made a sudden swoop in the midst of your army, with taken speed, like the Ender at the time of destruction, wishing to burn, like Death with rod in hand.
Of his speed in battle, extreme speed, your men could not bear the force as he rushed, like Time at its hour seizing creatures with gaping mouth.
Then the army of the Bharatas, scorched in the battle by the great soul, driven by Bhima, scattered in fear, like masses of clouds by a great wind.
[Bhima said:] "Seeing the foes on every side, Vishoka, my mind is greatly tormented by anxiety; the king afflicted, Kiriti has not come; I have been born to many sorrows, charioteer.

This is the sorrow, charioteer, that the king of dharma went into the midst of the enemy, leaving me; I know neither that he is alive nor that he is dead, nor Bibhatsu; therefore my sorrow today is very great.
I shall destroy this raised-up force of the foe, supremely confident; having slain these assembled in the midst of battle I shall be pleased with you today.
Look at all my quivers and arrows: what shall remain of the arrows in my chariot, of what kind and how many are they? Know it clearly and tell me, charioteer."
[Vishoka said:] "Six times ten thousand arrows, hero, razor-arrows and broad-heads of that number, two thousand iron arrows, hero, and three thousand pradaras, Partha,
there remain weapons, Pandava, that a cart drawn by six oxen could not carry; know this, wise one; shoot thousands; you have wealth of mace, sword and arms."
[Bhima said:] "Charioteer, look at this battle today, which is dreadful, with sun lost, like the realm of death, by my fierce arrows loosed, splitting kings with swift speed.
Today it will be known to the kings, charioteer, down to the children: either Bhimasena sinks in battle, or alone he will be the conqueror of the Kurus in battle.
Let all the Kurus come out in battle, or let the worlds tell of me down to the children; I alone shall fell my enemies, or they all may torment Bhimasena.
Let the gods merely accomplish what I hope for and the highest deed; let Arjuna, slayer of foes, come here today, quick as Shakra invoked at a sacrifice.
Look at this Bharata army being torn apart; why do these kings flee? Clearly the wise Savyasachin, best of men, is covering this army with arrows.
See the banners fleeing, Vishoka, the elephants, horses and bands of foot-soldiers in battle, chariots shattered, struck by arrows and darts; see these chariot-warriors, charioteer.
The Kaurava army is filled again and again, being badly slain, devoured by Dhananjaya's arrows, swift as thunderbolts, like a peacock-feathered golden-winged ones.

These chariots, horses and elephants flee, trampling bands of foot-soldiers; all the Kauravas, bewildered, flee like elephants in fear of a forest fire; and the great elephants in the battle give out vast cries of "Alas," Vishoka."
[Vishoka said:] "All your desires are fulfilled, Pandava; the monkey-bannered one is seen amid the elephant force; from a blue cloud I saw lightning rising, and that quivering bow.
That monkey is seen on all sides, having climbed to the top of Dhananjaya's banner; this divine jewel shines on the diadem, bright as the sun.
See at his side, Bhima, the Devadatta of fair sound, white as cloud, in the hand of Janardana as he plunges into the enemy army.
See the discus of Janardana standing at his side, bright as the sun, with diamond hub and razor edge, increasing Keshava's fame, ever honoured by the Yadus, hero."
[Bhima said:] "I give you, charioteer, fourteen excellent villages, well pleased with this good news, a hundred female slaves and twenty chariots, that you tell me of Arjuna, Vishoka."
Hearing Arjuna's words, Govinda said to Arjuna, "I go very quickly to where Bhima is stationed."
He approached with horses the colour of snow and conch, bound with nets of gold, pearls and jewels, Jishnu wishing to slay Jambha, thunderbolt in hand, like Indra of fierce anger for victory.

Chariots, horses, elephants and bands of foot-soldiers, with the roar of arrows and the sound of wheel-rims and hooves, making the earth and quarters resound, enraged lions among men, advanced for victory.
The battle of them and Partha that took place there was great, the destruction of the sin of the body, like that of the god Vishnu, best of victors, with the asuras for the three worlds.
Thus bewildered, the charioteer entered the king's palace and saw the best of kings, lord whose eye is wisdom.
Reaching the banyan then, O king, those great chariot-warriors, best of men, saw that best of trees.

[Sanjaya said:] "O king, put aside your grief; you have heard the conclusions of the Vedas and the many scriptures from the elders, best of kings; and what the sages said of old to Srinjaya afflicted by grief for his son."
The son of Surya, whom Kunti told of at the water-oblation, possessed of all virtues, who was cast into the water long ago—
There is no anger in Brahmanas; whence anger or torment? Forgive from gentleness, good one; let this serpent be freed.
Grief greatly made in the mind, O lord of men, torments the ancestors and grandfathers who died before.
Dhrishtaketu's sister and Jarasandha's daughter, all the servants, attended Gandhari too.
Having said this, Hrishikesha entered his house again; the lord of the world did not wish to make Death otherwise.
The five brothers and Krishna as sixth, and a dog as seventh, with the king himself as seventh, set out from Hastinapura, followed far by the townspeople and all the women of the inner apartments.
What worlds do they have now? I wish to see them, and the great-souled Karna, son of Kunti, true to his promise—
